title: Counts to Magnitudes
subtitle: Why a star looks fainter low in the sky, how a night of standard stars turns counts into magnitudes, and what the calibration cannot tell you
body:
Step 1 of 6 read

A night of standard stars

A detector counts electrons; a catalog lists magnitudes. To turn one into the other an observer measures standard stars, stars whose magnitudes are already known, at several heights in the sky. Each point below is one measurement of one standard: the horizontal axis is the airmass (1 straight overhead, about 2 at 30 degrees above the horizon), the vertical axis how far the instrument’s own magnitude lies from the catalog’s.

The night is synthetic: made by a model from a stated truth, with noise, so the answer can be checked afterwards. Nobody observed it.

title: Counts to Magnitudes
subtitle: Why a star looks fainter low in the sky, how a night of standard stars turns counts into magnitudes, and what the calibration cannot tell you
body:
Step 6 of 6 read

What a calibration does

A night of standards fixes three numbers: the zero point (what magnitude one count per second is), the extinction of the air, and a color term (the instrument sees blue and red stars a little differently). With them, any star on the same frames gets a calibrated magnitude, with an uncertainty that comes from how well the night fixed them. The next steps make one. Remember the night is synthetic and the extinction is the atmosphere’s, not the dust’s.
